claims.text: The corrosion resistance of steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications is primarily governed by an in situ Cr-rich passive oxide film.
The Cr-rich passive oxide film forms rapidly under operational conditions.
The passive film dynamically self-heals after ion-induced damage.
The Cr-rich oxide film acts as a protective barrier against corrosive species.
A sufficient baseline Cr content enables alloy steel to form a passive oxide layer.
ETEM or an in situ spectroelectrochemical cell can be used to monitor oxide formation and repair under simulated corrosive and irradiated environments.
The governing structural mediator is a continuous, self-renewing Cr-rich passive oxide film.
Selective oxidation of Cr at the steel surface produces a Cr-enriched oxide film.
After mechanical or chemical disruption, immediate re-oxidation of accessible Cr atoms repairs the passive film.
Repair of the Cr-rich film maintains passivity and prevents further dissolution of the underlying metal.
Steels with adequate Cr will form a uniform, dense, and self-repairing passive layer under the simulated environments.
Steels with adequate Cr will have significantly lower localized corrosion rates than low-Cr steels.
Steels with adequate Cr will dynamically regenerate the oxide film after induced damage.
Steels with insufficient Cr will show more frequent film rupture and greater corrosion penetration under otherwise identical conditions.
A steel with an intentionally removed oxide layer will show greater subsequent corrosion penetration under otherwise identical conditions.
The hypothesis is expected to apply only within the tested chemical, temperature, and radiation regimes.
Cr is the principal passivation-forming element, while the effects of Ni and Co on passivity are limited.
The kinetics of passive-film self-healing under simultaneous radiation and chemical attack are uncertain.
Alloy microstructure and alloying elements may modify behavior under the proposed conditions.

contradictions.description: The mechanism predicts immediate repair after passive-film disruption when accessible Cr is present, whereas the baseline groups an intentionally oxide-stripped steel with insufficient-Cr steel and predicts greater corrosion without specifying that the stripped steel is also Cr-deficient. An oxide-stripped high-Cr steel should instead repassivate under the proposed mechanism.
